Complete Empirical Research Plan  
“Community Health Centers and Mortality among Older Americans, 1965-1979”

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Chosen method: Staggered Difference-in-Differences with an event-study extension.

Why it fits
• Roll-out of Community Health Centers (CHCs) occurred at different calendar years across counties—exactly the quasi-experimental staggered timing DID is designed for.  
• We observe long panels of county-level mortality before and after first exposure.  
• Event-study coefficients allow visual and statistical tests of the parallel-trends assumption and show dynamic effects (anticipation, fade-out).  
• Recent econometric advances (Callaway & Sant’Anna 2021; Sun & Abraham 2021; Goodman-Bacon 2021) correct the bias that arises in two-way-fixed-effects (TWFE) with heterogeneous treatment timing. We will implement one of these estimators.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
Treatedct = 1 for county c in year t if ≥1 federally funded Community Health Center is operating in that county in year t. Treatedct = 0 otherwise. Once a county is treated, it stays treated (absorbing).

Control group  
Counties that never receive a CHC over the sample window, plus counties that are not yet treated in pre-treatment years (“not-yet-treated” serve as additional controls until their own treatment date).

Treatment timing  
EventTimect = t – FirstCHCYearc  
• EventTime = 0 is the first full calendar year of CHC operation.  
• EventTime < 0 are leads (pre-treatment).  
• EventTime > 0 are lags (post-treatment).  
We will trim to leads −6 … −1 and lags 0 … +10.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel trends: In the absence of CHCs, mortality among older adults would have evolved similarly in treated and control counties.  
Plausibility: CHC allocation targeted poor areas, so raw trends may differ. Including county fixed effects, state-by-year fixed effects, county-specific pre-trends, and weighting by age-race structure helps, but we must still test.

A2. No anticipation: Mortality does not change in the run-up to the opening of a CHC (people cannot meaningfully alter mortality risk in advance).  
Plausibility: High for mortality; we will confirm with lead coefficients.

A3. Stable composition / SUTVA: County population composition and treatment status of one county do not directly affect outcomes in another (no spillovers).  
Plausibility: Short-distance spillovers could occur if residents of a control county use a neighboring CHC; we will test distance-based spillovers and, if needed, drop border counties or aggregate to commuting zones.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Main Threats and Mitigation
--------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Selective placement of CHCs into counties on worsening health trajectories.  
• Mitigation: (i) Event-study pre-trends; (ii) Include county-specific linear trends; (iii) Propensity-score or entropy-balance re-weighting so control counties resemble treated on pre-period characteristics.

T2. Concurrent War on Poverty or Medicare/Medicaid expansions.  
• Mitigation: Add controls for other federal programs (e.g., OEO funds per capita, Medicaid physician participation). State-by-year fixed effects soak up contemporaneous state policy variation.

T3. Migration response (older adults move toward counties with CHCs).  
• Mitigation: Control for county-level age-specific population counts (denominator) and test for changes in migration patterns using Census intercensal estimates. Run robustness with place-of-birth mortality files (NCHS) where county of birth, not residence, is recorded for a subset of deaths.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# Load packages
library(data.table)
library(fixest)            # TWFE and interactive fixed-effects
library(did)               # Callaway & Sant’Anna estimator
library(ggplot2)

# 1. Data loading ----------------------------------------------------
# Assume two CSV files: mortality.csv and chc_rollout.csv
mort <- fread("mortality.csv")      # county, year, deaths50plus, population50plus
chc  <- fread("chc_rollout.csv")    # county, first_chc_year

# 2. Merge and construct variables -----------------------------------
dt <- merge(mort, chc, by = "county", all.x = TRUE)
dt[, first_chc_year := ifelse(is.na(first_chc_year), 9999, first_chc_year)]
dt[, treated := as.integer(year >= first_chc_year)]
dt[, ever_treated := as.integer(first_chc_year != 9999)]
dt[, event_time := year - first_chc_year]     # years relative to treatment
dt[, mort_rate := deaths50plus / population50plus * 1e5]  # per 100,000

# 3. Callaway & Sant’Anna DID ---------------------------------------
cs_out <- att_gt(yname = "mort_rate",
                 tname = "year",
                 idname = "county",
                 gname = "first_chc_year",   # group = first treatment year
                 xformla = ~ factor(state),  # state fixed effects
                 data = dt[year %between% c(1965,1979)],
                 panel = TRUE)

agg_simple <- aggte(cs_out, type = "group")

summary(agg_simple)

# 4. Event-study (Sun & Abraham with fixest) -------------------------
# Create relative-time dummies, omit -1 as reference
for(k in -6:10){
  dt[, paste0("rel",k) := as.integer(event_time == k)]
}

# keep only counties that will or never treat (not stagger >79)
dt2 <- dt[event_time >= -6 & event_time <= 10]

fe_es <- feols(mort_rate ~ i(event_time, ever_treated, ref = -1) |
               county + year, data = dt2,
               weight = ~(population50plus))

iplot(fe_es)  # ggplot of event-study

# 5. Robustness check: drop counties within 25 miles of a treated county -------
# Pre-computed distance matrix “county_neighbors”
nb <- fread("county_neighbors_25mi.csv")  # county, neighbor, within25
border_ctys <- unique(nb[within25 == 1 & county %in% dt[ever_treated==1, county], neighbor])
dt_rb <- dt[! county %in% border_ctys]

cs_out_rb <- att_gt(yname="mort_rate", tname="year", idname="county",
                    gname="first_chc_year", data=dt_rb, panel=TRUE)
summary(aggte(cs_out_rb, type="group"))
```
The code (i) loads and merges data, (ii) constructs treatment variables, (iii) estimates the staggered DID using the did package, (iv) runs a Sun-Abraham style event study with fixest, and (v) conducts a spillover robustness check by dropping border counties.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Direction: I expect CHCs to reduce mortality among persons aged 50+. Mechanisms include improved management of chronic diseases (hypertension, diabetes), access to preventive services, and referral to hospitals.

Magnitude (back-of-the-envelope): Baseline all-cause mortality for ages 50+ in the 1960s ≈ 2,500 per 100,000. If CHCs reduced mortality by 2–3 %, we would observe a fall of roughly 50–75 deaths per 100,000 in treated counties within 5 years.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
C1. Correctly specified treatment and timing …………………… 1  
C2. Parallel pre-trends visually and statistically supported …… 0.5  (to be tested)  
C3. No interference / spillovers between units ………………… 0.5  
C4. No simultaneous shocks differentially correlated with roll-out 0.5  
C5. Appropriate estimator for staggered timing ………………… 1  

Total = 3.5 / 5. The design is promising but hinges on convincing pre-trend evidence and addressing possible spillovers and other War-on-Poverty programs.
